rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of missing late compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether the critical pair remains fully resolved in a faster method.

The critical pair responds strongly to gradient slope, so test the intermediate duration of 8 minutes. This should recover full resolution while eluting the last peak sooner than the maximum-scoring initial method.

The 8-minute gradient retains maximum CRF, although its critical pair has little resolution margin. Raise temperature alone to test whether faster elution and a favorable selectivity shift can preserve full resolution.

Trim the gradient window and shorten its duration while keeping the slope close to the fully resolved 50 C run. Starting below the estimated first-peak elution composition should reduce elapsed time without making the early peaks unretained.

Shift the starting composition upward and trim the endpoint while preserving approximately the successful gradient slope. This tests a shorter method with the endpoint still comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Reduce the endpoint by one grid step to make the gradient shallower and recover the small resolution deficit in the critical pair. The last peak should remain inside the gradient, with full resolution potentially restored at a shorter elution time than injection 5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce elution time, while the narrower window makes the gradient shallower. Check whether the early pair stays retained and the critical middle pair preserves full resolution.

With maximum-CRF methods secured, test a much steeper gradient for a faster, alternative separation regime. The strong slope sensitivity of the middle pair suggests it may cross and separate again in reversed order; the low starting organic fraction protects early retention.

Explore the fast-gradient regime with a higher starting organic fraction and lower temperature to shift the critical pair’s selectivity. Lower temperature should also increase early retention, helping protect the first pair from compression.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to test whether the fast method’s critical middle pair gains separation in the reversed-order regime. The early pair has resolution margin, but both the middle and final pairs must improve to recover maximum CRF.

Return to the successful 50 C selectivity and test a compact two-minute gradient followed by a hold. This probes whether a faster slope and lower endpoint can shorten the fully resolved method, while checking the marginal middle pair and late-peak hold behavior.
Test whether a 5 C increase recovers the small middle-pair deficit of injection 6 while shortening elution. The early pair may lose resolution, so this run checks the temperature trade-off directly.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the early pair that limited injection 13. Keeping the endpoint and duration fixed modestly steepens the gradient, testing whether both critical pairs can remain fully resolved with a last peak near 3.4 minutes.

Test a narrower gradient window to preserve middle-pair resolution while advancing the starting composition. Lowering temperature to 45 C should help retain and separate the early pair, which may otherwise become too compressed.

Preserve injection 7’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope, but end the gradient earlier and use the final hold. This should preserve the critical middle separation while testing whether the late peaks can elute promptly at a lower final organic fraction.

With maximum CRF already secured, explore a higher-start, lower-temperature window for a faster alternative separation. The shallower slope should help the final pair, while this run tests whether altered selectivity can resolve the middle pair without collapsing early retention.

Refine the fastest fully resolved method, injection 8, by lowering the endpoint one step to improve its marginal middle-pair resolution. This tests whether a modest increase in elution time buys useful resolution margin while retaining maximum CRF.

Use the finer slope adjustment available with a six-minute gradient to bracket injections 6 and 7. The intermediate slope should recover full middle-pair resolution while bringing the last peak out sooner than injection 7.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 8 using the finer adjustment available with a six-minute gradient. This probes whether its small middle-pair resolution margin permits an even earlier last peak while retaining maximum CRF.
Back off the endpoint one grid step from injection 20 to restore full middle-pair resolution. This should retain a short elution time while providing slightly more resolution margin than injection 8.

Test a four-minute gradient with a lower starting fraction to improve early retention relative to injection 8. Its slope is shallower than injection 5’s, offering a promising combination of full resolution, useful resolution margin, and rapid elution.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a nearby method with more resolution margin. Lowering injection 7’s endpoint should improve the critical middle pair while keeping all six peaks well within ten minutes.

Test a 5 C decrease from injection 23 to improve early-pair separation while using its middle-pair resolution margin. This checks a nearby alternative expected to retain maximum CRF with all peaks eluting well before ten minutes.

Raise injection 24’s endpoint one grid step to shorten elution while spending some of its middle-pair resolution margin. This final refinement should preserve maximum CRF; injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.
